extracted.intended_audience: artists, art students, and the educated public (Victorian-era lecture audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A set of prescriptive aesthetic and moral criteria for judging, practising, and teaching the arts, given as a lecture-essay about what constitutes true art, the artist’s character, and the social effects of artistic labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts must have noble motive
rubrics_metrics.description: "The arts must have noble motive." (art prospers only when devoted to the proclamation of divine truth or law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin asserts that art should be rooted in a noble purpose—devotion to proclaiming divine truth or law—and that without such motive the arts cannot properly prosper. He warns that when abused art becomes "a curse to the earth" and serves pride and lust rather than higher ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should proclaim trustworthy truth, not deceive
rubrics_metrics.description: Art, when great, "strove to teach us something about the gods" but historically has often "betrayed their trust" in that proclamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: artistic work should aim at conveying trustworthy moral/spiritual insight; anti-patterns include grand imaginative display that misleads or trivializes sacred truths (e.g., turning religion into spectacle or sensuality). Ruskin critiques poets who play with ‘‘the most precious truths’’ and thereby misinform or deceive vast audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must awaken perception and counter apathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should rouse the heart, eyes, and ears—"lest the inspiration of hand or voice should reach us... and be healed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good art overcomes the "intense apathy" of audiences, awakening perception and encouraging moral and spiritual attention. An artwork's failure includes leaving audiences languid, unastonished, or indifferent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets and teachers should strive for plain, earnest truth about ultimate things
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest representatives (Dante and Milton) tried to "search out these deep things, and relate them"—the lecturer expects teachers to pursue and teach plainly and earnestly whatever can be known of the future destinies of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic claims about metaphysical or religious matters should be offered with seriousness and intellectual honesty rather than rhetorical ambiguity or fantastical play. Ruskin praises earnestness of thought and mastery of words but criticizes speculative or theatrical treatments that cannot be trusted by living faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should reveal universal human nature with compassionate insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Great artists like Homer and Shakespeare present the whole of human nature "in a pathetic weakness" or "mournful and transitory strength," often without personal anger or moral vindictiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: the best art has unoffended, uncondemning sight—revealing human weakness and strength with comprehension rather than mere rebuke or sentimentality. Ruskin elevates universality, psychological depth, and enduring formative influence as marks of high art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must not offer false consolation; it must confront moral complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (Achilles, Christian poet’s rendering) show that poetic treatment should not offer cheap comfort; greatness often records ruin, passion, and moral ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art judged by its courage to face human complexity honestly; anti-patterns include art that smooths over suffering with simplistic consolation or that substitutes melodrama for moral insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: True artistic skill is mostly in the doing, not the talking
rubrics_metrics.description: "The main thing I have to tell you is,—that art must not be talked about. The fact that there is talk about it at all, signifies that it is ill done, or cannot be done... The moment a man can really do his work he becomes speechless about it. All words become idle to him—all theories."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluating artists and teachers: competence is demonstrated by the work itself; verbosity, theory-making, or public talk often signal absence of real mastery. Good instruction in art is largely by example and practice (a silent guide), not by rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic mastery depends on instinct plus disciplined practice and science
rubrics_metrics.description: A great artist's power approximates animal instinct but is "added to an amount of practice, of science,—and of imagination disciplined by thought".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate artworks and artists by presence of an instinctive, well-practised technical ability, informed by scientific knowledge and disciplined imagination. Score higher where instinct is controlled and expanded by study and long labour; anti-patterns: mere virtuosity without disciplined thought, or pure theory without trained execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art is founded on dispositions created over generations and needs social conditions to flourish
rubrics_metrics.description: "The arts... differ from the sciences... their power is founded not merely on facts which can be communicated, but on dispositions which require to be created... Whole æras of mighty history are summed... in the existence of a noble art..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an art or attempting to revive it, account for its social and historical roots: true artistic vitality grows slowly across generations and under favourable social conditions; quick theoretical fixes or lectures cannot substitute for long cultural formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good work is receptive of correction; complacency signals arrested art
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between "corrigible Eve" (Lombardic) and "incorrigible Angel" (Irish): the Lombardic work shows a perception of beauty and law, struggling toward improvement; the Irish angel is complacent and ignorant of its failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: exemplary art shows awareness of imperfection and a striving for correction; artworks or schools that display complacency, refusal of critique, or satisfied self-satisfaction indicate a cultural or formal arrest and should be judged negatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: The artist’s moral disposition: humility combined with conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: "The more beautiful the art, the more it is essentially the work of people who feel themselves wrong... and yet, in still deeper sense, it is the work of people who know also that they are right."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate creators for a balance of self-critical humility (awareness of falling short) and steadfast adherence to a perceived law of beauty or truth. This tension—the persistent sense of failure amid a firm purpose—is a hallmark of the highest artistic achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worthily-followed industry and craftsmanship produce genuine happiness and moral value
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whenever the arts and labours of life are fulfilled in this spirit of striving against misrule... they invariably bring happiness..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art and craft that are pursued honourably and perfectly (honest workmanship) should be valued for their ethical as well as aesthetic rewards. In assessment, give weight to diligent, serviceable work (hewers of wood, drawers of water, artisans) because such work brings peace and fulfillment unlike mere ambition or passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and labour should produce tangible social benefit; failure to better life is a serious indictment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin catalogs the failures in agriculture, weaving, and building across six thousand years and contrasts the lost potential with the poets' visions of mercy, justice, and provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criterion for judging arts and related industries is their contribution to social welfare: do they relieve hunger, clothe the poor, and provide decent habitation? Anti-patterns include technical skill that results in social neglect (ruined fields, starvation, squalor) or splendid art that leaves real human needs unmet.
